Also flagged as a related hardening item regardless of approach: the deployed app auto-commits/pushes trip_log.csv on every log action - if both anglers log a catch at the same moment from separate devices, the second push could get rejected (non-fast-forward) the way we saw during a manual push tonight; the app's own auto-commit logic should pull-rebase-push with a retry so a genuinely simultaneous log from two phones never silently fails.

SOMEDAY/MAYBE - not for now, captured for later reference. Scoped after discussing true offline field-logging (dead-zone signal on the lake) and the possibility of eventually making this a public app with an upgraded look and feel. Confirmed Streamlit has no offline/PWA support at all (every interaction is a live round trip to the Python server - no official PWA toolkit, community consensus is it's not feasible) and that iOS Safari doesn't support the Background Sync API, so a real offline-capable field app means leaving Streamlit for a native/cross-platform mobile app (React Native or Flutter - one codebase for iOS+Android), with a local on-device database (SQLite) for full offline read/write and sync-on-reconnect, matching how real offline field-data tools (ODK Collect, ArcGIS Field Maps, Fulcrum) are all built as native apps, not web apps, for exactly this reason. Going public compounds the rebuild: (1) data layer - replace trip_log.csv-in-git with a real database (e.g. Postgres via Supabase/Neon) for genuine concurrent multi-user writes, real user accounts/auth replacing both Streamlit's lack of auth and the 'who's fishing' name tag, and a real API layer (FastAPI is a natural fit - the existing core/ scoring, lure, and weather logic is plain Python with no Streamlit dependency, so most of it carries over behind API endpoints rather than being rewritten); (2) the mobile app itself - offline-first field logging, camera/GPS via native APIs instead of browser widgets, app-store distribution and review cycles; (3) a separate public web frontend (real design system instead of Streamlit's default widget styling) for browsing forecasts/trip history without installing an app; (4) public-readiness hardening - rate limits/caching on external calls (Open-Meteo, USGS, USACE, Cabela's lookup, Claude vision lure-scanner) that are currently fine for 2 users but need real per-user caps at scale, real (non-free) hosting/ops, a privacy policy given anglers are protective of their spot locations, and a scope decision on single-lake (everything right now - bathymetry, shoreline, fish attractors - is Nolin-specific data) vs. multi-lake support. This is a genuine rebuild done as a different kind of project - months not days, with real staging/production environments and app-store release cycles - not an incremental feature on top of the current app. Revisit this item if/when ready to actually scope and start it.

Leaderboard periodically showed stale data, and a Streamlit Cloud reboot corrected it - twice. Root cause: get_trip_history()/get_calibrated_weights() (core/appstate.py, both a 5-minute st.cache_data) are read by Leaderboard, 7-Day Forecast, and Spot Session's own lure-recommendation panels, but unlike every other cached getter in this app (get_lake_spots, get_inventory, get_dev_tasks - each cleared right after its own page's write), neither was ever cleared after a trip write anywhere, across all 9 write sites in pages/6_Spot_Session.py and pages/4_Trip_History.py. A reboot masked this by starting a fresh process with a fresh cache. Fixed by clearing both caches at every write site (centralized in Spot Session's _push_or_toast() helper), and added a matching Refresh from GitHub button to Leaderboard (Trip History's existing one now clears these caches too, not just re-syncing the file). Separately confirmed: this morning's live session was lost the same way as the prior incident - the angler's reboot was a genuine Streamlit Cloud restart, which replaced the process's disk before that session's data ever reached GitHub. No written record exists; recreating from memory is in progress.

After swapping in a fresh PAT and rebooting, verified via a real Start Session / Cancel Session test that pushes still weren't reaching GitHub - zero new commits on the data branch, no visible toast either time. Root cause: github_token() reads st.secrets and returns empty on ANY problem (missing key, typo, a TOML syntax error elsewhere breaking the whole parse) with no signal beyond an easy-to-miss toast - so 'no token configured' and 'token configured but I can't tell' were indistinguishable from the UI. Added core.appstate.github_connection_status() and a persistent (not a toast) connection-status line on Spot Session (top of page) and Development (in an expander) - green + masked token preview if github_token() sees one, orange/red warning if not - so this is always checkable without depending on catching a toast. Separately, the Cancel Session confirm needing two clicks to take effect could not be reproduced in an isolated AppTest run of the exact click sequence (cancels correctly on the first confirm click every time) - left open as a likely client-side/network timing issue pending the token fix being confirmed.

Re-ran the Start/Cancel Session test with the new punch-list #62 connection indicator visible the whole time - it stayed 'connected' throughout, yet the push still never reached GitHub (confirmed via git log on the data branch: no new commits) and the Cancel Session double-click issue persisted. Root cause of the false confidence: github_connection_status() only checks whether github_token() returns a non-empty string - it can't distinguish a garbage/revoked/wrong-scope token from a genuinely working one, since that requires an actual round trip to GitHub. Added core.appstate.test_github_push_access(token, slug) - a real on-demand GitHub API request against the repo, interpreting the response the same way this session diagnosed the two previous bad tokens by hand with curl (401 = invalid/revoked, 200 with permissions.push: false = valid but read-only, permissions.push: true = genuinely working). Wired into a new 'Test connection now' button in Development's GitHub connection expander.

Live-tested the reported "pushes never reach GitHub despite a valid, push-capable token" and "Cancel Session needs two clicks" issues directly on the deployed app via browser automation (the angler asked me to reproduce them myself rather than keep relying on descriptions). FIXED (2026-09-03): Root-caused and fixed - user report: "trip history reverts to a last entry date of 8/23/2026" again, right after this session pushed several code fixes to main. Confirmed the real data branch was completely fine (136 rows through 9/2-9/3); the live app was instead serving mains own frozen data/trip_log.csv snapshot (73 rows, last date exactly 8/23) from the punch-list #52 cutover. Cause: app.pys once-per-boot data sync (sync_data_from_data_branch(), guarded by st.cache_resource) unconditionally cached success even when the sync itself failed - a single failed attempt (plausible right at cold boot, before a freshly started containers network is necessarily warmed up) permanently stranded that process on stale/frozen data for its whole life, with nothing retrying it. This sessions own back-to-back redeploys (#69/#70/#71/#72) made hitting that fluke on one boot far more likely than usual. Fixed two ways: sync_data_from_data_branch() (core/storage.py) now retries a transient network failure a few times with backoff before giving up (same pattern commit_and_push() already uses, punch-list #58); app.pys _sync_data_once() now raises instead of returning True on a still-unsuccessful result, so st.cache_resource does not memoize the failure - the next page load retries instead of being stuck for good. Verified via pytest (385 passed, 2 new regression tests confirmed to fail pre-fix/pass post-fix), a full AppTest smoke test across every page, and a targeted scratch AppTest script driving app.py through 4 consecutive reruns with the sync mocked to fail twice then succeed - confirmed the retry happens (the actual fix) AND that a successful sync still only runs once (no regression to punch-list #52s once-per-boot guarantee). If youre seeing stale data on the live app right now, the Refresh from GitHub button on Trip History/Tackle Box fixes it immediately regardless of any code deploy. Full writeup: SESSION_NOTES.md entry 140.

FIXED (2026-09-03): User report with a screenshot - a Tackle Box lure photo overlapped the neighboring cards info. One shared function, so every caller is fixed at once. Verified via pytest (387 passed, 2 new regression tests in tests/test_ui.py confirmed to fail pre-fix/pass post-fix), a full AppTest smoke test across every page, and a direct AppTest render of the real Tackle Box page confirming the actual card markup (55 real cards) now uses the responsive shape. FIXED (2026-09-03): User report - picking a lure/trailer from a dropdown cut off the text on mobile ("It is fine on a full scree computer, but not on my phone"), plus asked to check for other instances. Root cause confirmed live via Playwright at a real phone viewport (390x844), reproducing the exact bug: Streamlit 1.63.0 renders st.selectbox's CLOSED value through a React Aria ComboBox <input role="combobox">, a different element from the [data-baseweb="select"] dropdown-list div punch-list #33's existing mobile CSS already targets (that CSS still correctly handles the OPEN list, unaffected by this bug). That input had no text-overflow/overflow rule, so a long value (the Trailer picker's "Brand - Product - Color, size" labels run 50-90+ characters - the only selectbox in the app that long; everything else tops out ~29-34 chars) hard-clipped mid-character with no ellipsis. Fixed in core.ui.inject_mobile_css(): that input now gets overflow:hidden, text-overflow:ellipsis, AND white-space:nowrap (confirmed live that ellipsis alone does nothing without nowrap - the browser never treats a wrapping value as overflowing), applied everywhere since it is a strict improvement, plus a smaller font-size scoped to the mobile media query so more of a long value fits before truncating at all. Also confirmed live, separately, that the ellipsis only paints once the field loses focus - normal, universal browser behavior for every text input (a focused field scrolls to keep the caret visible instead), not a bug. Because the fix lives in the one shared CSS helper every page calls, it covers every selectbox app-wide going forward, not just the Trailer picker that reproduced the bug. Verified via pytest (389 passed, 2 new regression tests in tests/test_ui.py confirmed to fail pre-fix/pass post-fix), a full AppTest smoke test across every page, and by re-running the live Playwright repro against the fixed code and confirming via computed-style inspection that the value now actually renders with "..." once blurred, instead of the prior hard mid-character cut. Full writeup: SESSION_NOTES.md entry 142.

FIXED (2026-09-03): Live incident - user report while actively fishing: "I set everything up for a session this morning and started to fish. When I click on a lure to enter a fish I caught I got no response. It seems frozen...". Immediate guidance: nothing already logged was at risk (every catch saves to local disk immediately, before any network push, and Spot Session rebuilds its in-progress view from disk on reload, not browser memory - punch-list #29/#69) - user confirmed reloading recovered the session correctly. Root cause: every git subprocess call in core/storage.py (fetch, push, commit, add, worktree setup) had NO timeout. This app is used standing at a lake, often on weak/dropping cell signal - exactly the condition that makes a network call stall (never come back) rather than fail cleanly. Since every interaction here is a live, synchronous Streamlit script run with no background/async work, one stalled git process blocked that whole run - freezing the ENTIRE page, not just the action that triggered it - for as long as the connection stayed down, potentially indefinitely. Fixed: every git call now passes a real timeout (20s for fetch/push, 15s for local-only git plumbing). A new _run_git_or_timeout() helper turns a timed-out push/fetch into an ordinary failed result whose stderr matches an already-recognized transient-network-error marker, so it is automatically retried exactly like any other flaky-connection failure, with zero changes to the existing retry logic. commit_and_push()/push_pending()'s except clauses widened from CalledProcessError to SubprocessError (TimeoutExpired's parent) so a timeout returns a clean (False, message) instead of crashing uncaught. sync_data_from_data_branch() (punch-list #73's retry loop) needed no logic changes at all - its existing except Exception already caught anything, including a timeout, once timeout= was added to its calls. _ensure_data_worktree() now falls back to a local branch when its first fetch times out, instead of failing the save outright, so a commit can still happen locally and push later via the autosave retry heartbeat. Verified via pytest (394 passed, 5 new regression tests simulating hangs via subprocess.TimeoutExpired, confirmed via a targeted git stash that 4/5 fail pre-fix and all 5 pass post-fix - the 5th correctly passes both ways since #73's retry loop already handled generic exceptions), and a full AppTest smoke test across every page. Not live-reproduced against a real dropped connection (impractical from a coding session with no access to the live deployment's network) - verified at the unit level against simulated hangs exercising the same code path a real timeout would. Full writeup: SESSION_NOTES.md entry 143.

FIXED (2026-09-04): Follow-up to punch-list #73 - user reported the 8/23 Trip History reversion 'happens on every update we do' even after #73 shipped. Root cause: #73 fixed sync_data_from_data_branch() itself (retrying instead of permanently giving up on one bad boot), but missed a SEPARATE caching layer sitting on top of it - core.appstate's cached getters (get_trip_history(), get_calibrated_weights(), get_inventory(), get_lake_spots(), get_dev_tasks(), get_anglers(), get_water_quality_log(), get_spots()) are their own independent st.cache_data caches, up to 5 minutes for the trip-related ones, completely unaware of whether the file underneath them just got overlaid by a sync. A page render that happened to call one of these before a process's sync succeeded (a window #73 shrank but can't make zero) got its stale read memoized for its own full TTL regardless of the sync catching up moments later - this is what made a manual 'Refresh from GitHub' still sometimes necessary even though the underlying file was already correct. Fixed in app.py: _sync_data_once() now clears every one of those data-backed getters the instant a sync actually succeeds (not on every attempt - only the one real success per process). Considered and rejected a deeper fix (untracking data/*.csv from main entirely, removing the frozen-snapshot fallback) at the user's explicit request to look for 'the real fix' - rejected because the frozen main snapshot is a deliberate, valuable fallback (lets the app boot and run even if the data branch or GitHub itself is unreachable), and the reversion was never that fallback being wrong, only this separate cache never learning a sync had succeeded. Verified via pytest (396 passed, 2 new AppTest-based regression tests in the new tests/test_app.py confirmed to fail pre-fix/pass post-fix), and a full AppTest smoke test across every page. Full writeup: SESSION_NOTES.md entry 144.

FIXED (2026-09-04): Live-reproduced right after a redeploy: Trip History showed main's frozen 8/23 snapshot again, but clicking 'Refresh from GitHub' (the exact same sync function, same arguments as the automatic boot sync) fixed it instantly - ruling out network/auth/repo problems and pointing at the automatic retry budget being too short. sync_data_from_data_branch()'s old defaults (max_retries=3, retry_backoff_seconds=1.0) gave a fast-failing transient error only about 3 seconds of total backoff before giving up for that whole script run - not enough for a real Streamlit Community Cloud cold boot's network warm-up, evidently. Raised to max_retries=6, retry_backoff_seconds=2.0 (~30s total retry window); a non-transient failure still fails fast, unaffected. Also added core.storage.last_boot_sync_status, a process-global record of the boot sync's real outcome (ok/message/timestamp), surfaced on the Development page's GitHub connection panel - so a fourth occurrence, if it ever happens, is diagnosable from the actual error text immediately instead of another round of guessing from symptoms. Live-verified on the very next redeploy: Trip History showed the correct, current date range automatically, with no manual refresh needed, and the new diagnostic confirmed a successful automatic sync. Verified via pytest (399 passed, 1 new regression test that deliberately calls the function with no overrides - unlike every existing #73-era retry test, which all pass explicit overrides and would stay green regardless of the real defaults - confirmed to fail against the old default of 3 and pass against the fix of 6), and a full AppTest smoke test across every page. Full writeup: SESSION_NOTES.md entry 146.
